content.content:
## Extraction integrity

Never trust working memory for a figure, amount, date, or quote you're
about to write onto a page. If the fact came from a saved raw source
(an ingested transcript, article, or captured email), re-read it from that
file at the moment of writing rather than recalling it from earlier in the
conversation — long-context recall degrades and transposes digits in ways
that silently corrupt exactly the kind of data this skill exists to merge
carefully.

## Preview before writing

Findings and proposed merges are informational until confirmed — this skill
never auto-applies a revision, the same way the rest of wakil's write path
never does. `ingest_service.py`'s enrichment DAG and
`schema_migrate_service.py`'s migration planner both split into a
plan/propose phase that touches nothing and a separate apply phase that
only runs after confirmation (`schema_migrate_service` even re-reads each
file immediately before writing and skips any file that changed since
planning, rather than overwriting it blind). Follow the same shape here:
produce the diff, show what's additive vs. what's flagged as a conflict,
and only write once that's confirmed.

## Provenance and timestamps

- Update the `updated:` frontmatter field (present on identity-type schemas
  such as `person`/`company`, alongside `created:`) when a revision lands —
  don't leave it stale after a real content change.
- Never invent or leave a placeholder date. If the new fact's date isn't
  known, say so explicitly rather than writing "recently" or today's date
  as a guess.
- Never replace a developed note with a freshly generated summary, even
  when the summary is accurate — a shorter, cleaner-looking page that drops
  prior detail is the clobbering bug wearing a different outfit.

Once the merge is written and confirmed, hand off to `note-conformance` for
the shape/schema pass, then `kb-commit` to land it.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("src/wakil/skills/note-revision/SKILL.md")
s = p.read_text()
anchor = "## Preview before writing"
assert anchor in s
new = '''## Don't fill a gap with invented detail

A real gap in the source is worth naming. Filling it with plausible-sounding
specifics is not, and is harder to catch than an ordinary mistake because
the invented detail reads as corroboration.

A transcript with a genuine diarization failure produced prose that went
well beyond "diarization failed": it asserted a specific tool's internal
behaviour, quoted verbatim noise tokens, and gave a precise call duration
that was wrong by four minutes — none of which appeared anywhere in the
input. The underlying gap was correctly identified; everything layered on
top of it to make the observation concrete was fabricated.

So:

- State the gap in the terms the source actually supports, and stop there.
  "All 41 segments from the other participant came back near-empty" is
  supportable if you counted them. "MacWhisper only enrolled one speaker
  profile" is a claim about a tool you cannot see.
- Never supply illustrative examples — sample tokens, representative
  quotes, round numbers — unless you are copying them from the input.
- A number you did not read in the source (a duration, a count, a
  percentage) does not belong on the page. Precision is read as evidence.

## Never assert what a source does *not* contain

You may be looking at part of the source. When the input is truncated you
are told so explicitly, and in that case a claim of the form "X is not
discussed here" is unsupportable no matter how confident it feels.

Even without truncation, prefer describing what the source *does* say.
"The recording covers A and B" is verifiable; "the recording never mentions
C" requires having seen all of it and is exactly the kind of claim that has
turned out to be false about content that was present but out of view.

## Pronouns: don't infer them

Write about a person using the pronouns their own page states. If the page
has no `pronouns:`/`gender:` field and the source doesn't specify, use
they/them, or restructure around the person's name.

Do not infer pronouns from a first name, a role, a voice, or context. A
default guess is wrong roughly as often as it is right, it lands in durable
prose across several pages at once, and it is tedious for the reader to
correct after the fact. Neutral phrasing costs nothing when the information
genuinely isn't available.

## Preview before writing'''
p.write_text(s.replace(anchor, new, 1))
PYEOF

content.content:
---
name: transcript
description: Judgment for extracting knowledge from meeting transcripts.
skill_api: 1
---

You are analyzing a meeting transcript that has already been captured raw.
Your job is judgment, not cleanup: what was decided, by whom, and what it
changes.

- Find the resolution, not the first option. Meetings circle: an idea raised
  early is often discarded later. Anchor on where the discussion *landed* —
  the last clear statement of a decision wins over the first proposal.
- Attribute claims to speakers. "Jane committed to the routing design" is a
  usable memory; "the routing design was discussed" is not. Use the
  user-provided context (attendees, company, purpose) to resolve first names
  and pronouns to full names.
- Watch joint-pronoun language as a structural signal, not filler. "We hold
  them responsible," "you, me, we," "between us" usually means both parties
  share the accountability, not just the one the sentence's subject
  foregrounds. A memory or decision that lands the obligation on only one
  side when the transcript used joint-pronoun language is worth a second
  read before writing it down.
- Separate decisions from open questions. A decision has an owner and a
  next step; anything still contested belongs in a question-type memory, not
  a decision.
- On top of the fact-vs-opinion distinction given elsewhere in this request:
  casually-asserted 1:1 claims (an off-the-cuff metric, a provocative
  aside, something hedged or jokey) get low `confidence` (guidance: ≤0.4)
  and `stance="casual"` even when phrased fact-like — never silently
  upgrade a hot take to a confident, formal-register fact. `stance` (the
  claim's register/commitment level) is independent of `type`: a casual
  opinion and a casual fact are both valid.
- Date what happened. Memories describing dated events (the meeting itself,
  a committed deadline, an announced change) are event-type memories carrying
  the event's own date — not the date you are writing this.
- Quote pivotal exchanges verbatim in the proposed note where the exact
  wording matters (commitments, disagreements, numbers); paraphrase the rest.
- Link entities — people, companies, concepts, projects, prior meetings — to
  the existing related notes with [[wikilinks]] where they genuinely match;

# Source truncation is no longer silent (issue #176)


def test_a_short_source_is_untouched():
    from wakil.app.ingest_service import _truncate_source

    proposal = EnrichmentProposal(source_id=1, title="Short")
    assert _truncate_source("brief text", proposal) == "brief text"
    assert proposal.warnings == []


def test_a_truncated_source_warns_the_operator_and_tells_the_model():
    """Issue #176's root cause: a ~28-minute transcript exceeded
    MAX_SOURCE_CHARS and was silently cut, so the model correctly reported
    that content was 'not present in the transcript' -- a true statement
    about the input it received, read as a false claim about the recording."""
    from wakil.app.ingest_service import MAX_SOURCE_CHARS, _truncate_source

    proposal = EnrichmentProposal(source_id=1, title="Long")
    long_text = "x" * (MAX_SOURCE_CHARS * 2)

    result = _truncate_source(long_text, proposal)

    # The model is told its view is partial, so it can't reason about absence.
    assert "SOURCE TRUNCATED" in result
    assert "Do not state or imply that anything is absent" in result
    assert result.startswith("x" * 100)
    # And the operator can see it happened, with the scale of the loss.
    assert len(proposal.warnings) == 1
    assert "truncated" in proposal.warnings[0]
    assert f"{MAX_SOURCE_CHARS:,}" in proposal.warnings[0]


def test_truncation_notice_is_appended_not_substituted():
    """The budget still has to be respected -- the notice is extra, and the
    analyzed prefix must be exactly what it was before."""
    from wakil.app.ingest_service import MAX_SOURCE_CHARS, _truncate_source

    proposal = EnrichmentProposal(source_id=1, title="Long")
    long_text = "abcdefghij" * (MAX_SOURCE_CHARS // 5)
    result = _truncate_source(long_text, proposal)
    assert result[:MAX_SOURCE_CHARS] == long_text[:MAX_SOURCE_CHARS]

content.content:
## Procedure

- [ ] Step 1: **Read the existing note in full before writing anything.**
      Load its current State, Timeline, and frontmatter. You cannot
      classify a change as additive, contradicting, or duplicate against
      content you haven't read.
- [ ] Step 2: **Re-read the raw source for the new facts, not your memory
      of it.** See "Extraction integrity" below — never transcribe a
      figure, date, or quote from earlier in a conversation when the saved
      raw source is available to re-read at the moment of writing.
- [ ] Step 3: **Classify the new material** against what's already on the
      page: additive, contradicting/superseding, or a duplicate. See "The
      three-tier dedup heuristic" below.
- [ ] Step 4: **Apply the region-specific update discipline**:
      re-synthesize State, append to Timeline. Never regenerate the whole
      page from only the new source. See "State vs. Timeline" below. Carry

content.text: Now recording the generalizable lesson — this is exactly what `DEVELOPMENT.md` exists for:

input.command:
cat >> docs/DEVELOPMENT.md <<'MDEOF'

### A budget-capped model input must announce the cap in both directions

**Established:** 2026-08-07 · **Source:** issue #176, `_truncate_source` in `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`; second instance of the shape recorded at `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`'s "Workspace guide file (RESOLVER.md) is silently truncated at 4,000 chars"

`prepare_enrichment` cut its source at `MAX_SOURCE_CHARS` (24,000) with `text[:MAX_SOURCE_CHARS]` and said nothing to anyone. A ~28-minute transcript exceeded that, so the model wrote that a topic "is not present in the captured transcript here" — a *true* statement about the input it received, which the operator read as a false claim about their own recording and filed as a synthesis-accuracy bug. The model was right and the tool was wrong.

This is the second recorded instance of the same shape (RESOLVER.md's 4,000-char cut was the first), so it is worth stating as a rule rather than a fix: **any place a budget cap trims model input needs two announcements, not one.**

- **Tell the model**, inline in the text it receives, that its view is partial and what it must not conclude from that. A cap that is invisible to the model licenses exactly the reasoning-about-absence that caused this: it cannot distinguish "not in the source" from "not in my slice of the source."
- **Tell the operator**, on the proposal/result, with the scale of the loss. "Summary of a 28-minute call seems thin" is not diagnosable; "truncated to 24,000 of 61,400 characters" is.

Append the notice rather than substituting it into the budget, and assert in a test that the analyzed prefix is byte-identical to what it was before — otherwise a fix for visibility quietly shrinks the input it was meant to explain.

### Adding SKILL.md guidance has a budget cost that can degrade an unrelated step

**Established:** 2026-08-07 · **Source:** issue #176, `note-revision/SKILL.md`, four measured live-eval runs

Adding three sections and one procedure step to `note-revision/SKILL.md` (197 → 257 lines) made the new pronoun scenario pass and made an **unrelated, pre-existing** scenario fail — `no-existing-note-handoff-to-content-synthesis`, whose failing rubric item is about accurately enumerating the workspace's files during Step 1. Measured, not assumed: 3/3 failures on the edited skill, 1/1 pass on `main`'s version of the same file, same day.

Two rounds of tuning followed, and each fixed one failure by causing the other:

| variant | lines | pronoun scenario | handoff scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| new step + sections mid-file | 257 | pass | **fail** |
| compressed prose | 233 | pass | **fail** |
| scan folded into an existing step, sections moved to end | 230 | **fail** | pass |
| dedicated step restored, sections at end | 231 | pass | (regression stands) |

Two things to take from this. First, **a skill's instruction budget is real** — guidance is not free to add, and the cost lands on whichever step is competing for attention, not necessarily on anything topically related to what you added. Budget an eval run for scenarios you did *not* touch, not just the one you wrote. Second, the third row is the same finding already recorded above under "Check whether a skill's own procedure step order can produce the bug it's trying to prevent": demoting the pronoun scan from its own numbered step to a clause inside another step broke it. A gate needs to be a step.

Stopping after two rounds was deliberate, per this file's own entry on the personal-reflection heuristic: when each round of tuning trades one failure for another, the approach is the problem, not the tuning. The remaining regression is on a picky file-enumeration rubric item and is documented in the PR rather than tuned against.
MDEOF
uv run pytest -q 2>&1|tail -3; uv run ruff check 2>&1|tail -2; uvx ty check . 2>&1|tail -2

🐛 fix(enrich): stop truncating sources silently; tighten synthesis rules

#176 reported that enrichment claimed content was "not present in the
transcript" when it demonstrably was. The root cause is not a synthesis
failure: `prepare_enrichment` cut its input at MAX_SOURCE_CHARS (24,000)
with a bare slice and told nobody. A ~28-minute transcript exceeded that, so
the model made a true statement about the input it received, which read as a
false claim about the recording. The model was right; the tool was wrong.

- `_truncate_source` appends an explicit notice to the text the model sees,
  saying its view is partial and that it must not reason about absence, and
  records a warning on the proposal with the scale of the loss. The notice
  is appended, not substituted, so the analyzed prefix is byte-identical to
  before -- there is a test for that.

The other two failure modes in that issue are model-behaviour, so they land
in the skills of the DAG stages that actually write the prose:

- `note-revision` and `entity-compile` gain a pronoun rule framed as what it
  is -- a gendered pronoun is a factual claim needing a source, and that
  source is the person's own `pronouns:`/`gender:` field, never a name, role,
  or context. `note-revision` gets an explicit scan step, because the eval
  showed the rule stated as prose alone doesn't hold.
- `note-revision` and `transcript` gain a don't-invent-illustrative-detail
  rule (the reported case fabricated noise tokens, a tool's internals, and a
  wrong-by-four-minutes duration on top of a real, correctly-identified gap),
  and a don't-assert-absence rule.

New eval scenarios for both rules, run live per docs/adr/0004: both pass.

Known regression, measured not assumed: the pre-existing
`note-revision/no-existing-note-handoff-to-content-synthesis` scenario now
fails one of six rubric items (accurate file enumeration during Step 1) --
3/3 on this branch, 1/1 pass on main's version of the file, same day. Two
rounds of tuning each traded that failure for the pronoun one; per this
repo's own guidance on heuristics that swap failure modes, the tuning
stopped there rather than continuing. DEVELOPMENT.md records both the
truncation rule and the instruction-budget finding.

Closes #176

Closes #176.

> **Stacked on #201** → #200 → #199 → #198 → #197 → #194.

## The headline finding: this was wakil's bug, not the model's

#176 reports that enrichment claimed content was *"not present in the captured transcript here"* when the transcript demonstrably contained it. That reads as a synthesis-accuracy failure. It isn't.

`prepare_enrichment` cut its input with a bare `text[:MAX_SOURCE_CHARS]` (24,000 chars) and told **nobody** — not the operator, not the model. A ~28-minute / 415-segment transcript exceeds that comfortably. So the model made a **true statement about the input it actually received**, which the operator read as a false claim about their recording.

`_truncate_source` now announces the cap in both directions: an inline notice telling the model its view is partial and that it must not reason about absence, and a warning on the proposal with the scale of the loss. The notice is **appended, not substituted** — a test asserts the analyzed prefix is byte-identical to before, so a visibility fix can't quietly shrink the input it exists to explain.

This is the second instance of this shape (RESOLVER.md's silent 4,000-char cut was the first), so `DEVELOPMENT.md` records it as a rule.

## The two genuine model-behaviour issues

Placed in the skills of the DAG stages that actually write the prose, per `DEVELOPMENT.md`'s warning that guidance in the wrong stage can't fix anything:

- **Pronouns** (`note-revision`, `entity-compile`) — framed as what it actually is: *a gendered pronoun is a factual claim about a person and needs a source, and that source is their own `pronouns:`/`gender:` field.* Not a first name, not a role, not context.
- **Invented detail + absence claims** (`note-revision`, `transcript`) — the reported case fabricated verbatim noise tokens, a tool's internal behaviour, and a duration wrong by four minutes, layered on top of a real and correctly-identified gap.

## What the live evals actually showed

New scenarios for both rules; **both pass**. Two things worth your attention:

**The prose-only version of the pronoun rule did not work.** First run, the model *cited* my invented-detail rule while writing "his side" and "every one of his lines" about a person whose page states no pronouns. It only held once the scan became its own numbered procedure step — the step-ordering lesson already in `DEVELOPMENT.md`, confirmed again.

**There is a measured regression, and I'm flagging rather than burying it.** The pre-existing `note-revision/no-existing-note-handoff-to-content-synthesis` scenario now fails 1 of 6 rubric items — accurate workspace file enumeration during Step 1, topically unrelated to anything I added. Measured, not assumed:

| variant | lines | pronoun | handoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| new step + sections mid-file | 257 | pass | **fail** (3/3) |
| compressed prose | 233 | pass | **fail** |
| scan folded into existing step, sections at end | 230 | **fail** | pass |
| **shipped:** dedicated step, sections at end | 231 | pass | **fail** |

`main`'s version of the file passes that scenario 1/1 the same day, so this is a real regression, not the baseline flakiness `docs/adr/0004` describes. (Though that flakiness is real too — `additive-merge-happy-path` failed and then passed across two runs with byte-identical content.)

Two rounds of tuning each traded one failure for the other. Per this repo's own recorded guidance on heuristics that swap failure modes — *"the approach itself, not the tuning, was the problem"* — I stopped there rather than continuing to tune against a picky rubric item. **Your call whether that trade is acceptable**; the alternative is dropping the pronoun scan step, which measurably breaks the fix this PR is for.

`DEVELOPMENT.md` records the instruction-budget finding, since "adding guidance is not free, and the cost lands on whichever step is competing for attention" is not obvious and cost real API budget to establish.

## Verification

`675 passed`, `ruff check` clean, `ty check` clean, `wakil skills lint`/`validate` clean.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

input.content:
wakil · repair log · August 2026

The tool was quietly telling you it worked

Thirty-six open issues, filed mostly from one painful week of real use. They weren't thirty-six bugs. They were a handful of failures that compounded — and almost every one of them failed silently, which is why fixing them changes what the whole tool feels like.

14issues closed
10pull requests
675tests passing

wakīl means an entrusted agent — one authorized to act on your behalf. That framing turns out to be the right lens on this batch, because none of these bugs crashed. They reported success. A commit landed on main while printing a branch name. A transcript came out with two frontmatter blocks. An enrichment exited 0 having written nothing at all. Every one of them needed you to independently check the work.

Here's what actually changed, ordered by how much it was costing you.

Your commits stop going somewhere else

Tier 1

This is the one that mattered most, because until it was true nothing downstream could be trusted. land_ingestion committed to whatever HEAD happened to be at that instant, then printed the branch it intended. That message was a label, not an observation.

Was Committed d437dba430 on wakil/ingest/…-engineer-a $ git branch --contains d437dba430 main
Now Refusing to commit: expected to be on 'wakil/ingest/…-engineer-a', but HEAD is on 'main'. The written files are still on disk; nothing was committed.

Three related failures had the same shape — a remembered value trusted where reality should have been checked. gh pr create ran without --head, so GitHub inferred the branch from whatever was checked out; that's why an Engineer B ingest errored citing Engineer G's branch. And the "returned to…" branch was frozen at the start of the run, so enrich dropped you on a stale branch from some earlier command.

Underneath all of it: nothing stopped two wakil processes sharing one checkout. You found the culprit yourself — orphaned wakil mcp serve processes from earlier sessions, driving git on their own. There's now a lock, and it names the offending pid.

#181 commits reaching main #180 wrong-branch PRs #182 concurrent sessions #171 signing timeout

What to expect

You can stop running git branch --contains after every enrichment. A lost race now fails loudly with a message that names what to do, instead of committing to the trunk and telling you otherwise. And a 10-minute commit budget means 1Password's signing prompt no longer kills a run halfway through — if it does time out, your work stays staged on the branch rather than needing reconstruction by hand.

Hand-cleaned transcripts survive contact with ingest

Tier 1

Six consecutive ingests, six hand-repairs. Capture read your .md whole and wrapped it — frontmatter, H1 and all — inside a second, emptier block, where every outer field was blank or a day off.

Was --- title: '2026-08-04: …' tags: '' company: '' --- # 2026-08-03-transcript-note --- title: "2026-08-03: AI-mentoring…" tags: [mentoring, acme] company: companies/acme ---
Now --- title: "2026-08-03: AI-mentoring…" tags: [mentoring, acme] company: companies/acme type: source captured: '2026-08-03' --- # 2026-08-03-acme-engineer-h

Your frontmatter is now authoritative; wakil fills only the gaps and keeps ownership of type:. The filename comes from the note's own title instead of whatever the scratch file was called — which, as you predicted in the issue thread, fell out of the same fix.

Two neighbours went with it. clean_transcript was running on hand-authored markdown, reducing every **[00:36]** marker to **** — it's now skipped entirely for files that carry their own frontmatter or H1. And dates came from datetime.now(UTC) everywhere, so an 8:49pm Eastern capture got tomorrow's date. Calendar dates are local now; database timestamps stay UTC.

#172 double-wrap #179 stripped timestamps #174 dates a day ahead #173 silent -1 suffix #178 stale raw_text_path

What to expect

The dedupe-and-rename fixup after every transcript ingest goes away. So does the trap it led into: wakil index now follows a moved capture automatically, and wakil sources relink handles the case where the file was edited as well as moved. A destination collision is a clear error offering --overwrite, not a shadow copy at …-1.md.

An enrichment stops throwing away its own work

Tier 2

Two failures here were, in your words, inverted in severity. A mechanically-correctable path error hard-failed the entire run — four model calls discarded — while a substantive dropped output was silent.

Worse, wakil manufactured the first one itself: when a proposed page's path collided, the fallback dumped it into drafts/ ignoring its type: entirely, and the validator then rejected it for being in drafts/. A type: source page belongs in sources/; that's a pure function of one field, and it's now corrected with a warning — exactly like the filename half already was.

Was Proposal failed validation: ✗ type 'source' pages belong under sources/, not drafts/ Nothing was written.
Now warning: Moved the proposed note from drafts/… to sources/… to match its own `type:` Enriched source #27: 3 file(s)

The duplicate-page bug (#186) had a subtler cause than it looked. Every existing guard compared paths or resolution.name — and neither is a page's identity. proposed_frontmatter can override the name that actually gets written, so two files with byte-identical type: and name: passed every check. Deduplication now reads identity back out of the built content.

And #188 — a second source about the same topic resolving to a page that exists only on an earlier, unmerged branch — no longer exits 0 with nothing written. It names the branch holding the target and fails.

#187 run discarded over a path #186 duplicate pages #188 silent no-op #183 archive a dead source

The most interesting one: the model was right

Tier 2
Root cause found

You filed #176 because enrichment claimed a topic was "not present in the captured transcript here" when the transcript demonstrably contained it. That reads as a synthesis failure. It wasn't one.

prepare_enrichment cut its input at 24,000 characters with a bare slice and told nobody — not you, not the model. Your ~28-minute transcript exceeded that comfortably. So the model made a perfectly true statement about the input it actually received, and you read it as a false claim about your recording.

The cut still happens — it's a real budget — but it now announces itself in both directions. The model is told its view is partial and that it must not reason about absence. You get a warning naming the scale: truncated to 24,000 of 61,400 characters.

The other two halves of that issue were genuinely model behaviour, and went into the skill files for the pipeline stages that write the prose: a rule against inventing illustrative detail to make a real gap concrete (the fabricated noise tokens and the wrong-by-four-minutes duration), and a pronoun rule framed as what it actually is — a gendered pronoun is a factual claim about a person and needs a source, and that source is their own pronouns: field, not a first name or a role.

Worth knowing how that one was verified. Written as prose alone, it didn't hold: on the first live eval the model cited the invented-detail rule while still writing "his side" about someone whose page states no pronouns. It only stuck once the check became its own numbered step in the procedure.

Two corrections to the issues as filed

Findings
  • #179 is partly misfiled. A bare **00:36** never reproduced — neither regex matches it. Only the bracketed **[00:36]** form was destroyed. The em-dash always survived too. The test table covers all seven cases.
  • #168 isn't confirmed as the cause of the flakiness attributed to it in the comments. The intermittent "that file doesn't exist on disk" warnings have a separate, fully confirmed cause in #188. Worth re-testing before assuming the workspace-identity work will fix them.

What's still open

Honest status

Twenty-two issues remain, all mapped to lanes and branch names in the plan. None are in the data-integrity tier — that's finished.

AreaIssuesStatus
Git landing & isolation171, 180, 181, 182done
Capture correctness172, 173, 174, 179done
Enrichment proposals186, 187, 188done
Source lifecycle178, 183done
Synthesis accuracy176done
Workspace identity168planned
Force-retry dedup, required outputs170, 190planned
Whisper quality175needs a real fixture
New inputs (PDF, stdin, X)189, 131, 132planned
Memory & ranking122, 144, 145, 153planned
Indexing, context, QMD121, 154, 160, 166planned
Dream147, 148planned
Repo hygiene192planned
Deliberately deferred140, 146, 159, 167triage

One deliberate scope call worth surfacing: #175's premise doesn't hold as written. _dialogue_from_segments already merges consecutive same-speaker segments and emits paragraphs, not bullets. The evidence you pasted is consistent with MacWhisper's diarization flip-flopping mid-turn, which is a different problem. It needs a real .whisper archive in the test fixtures before anyone writes code, or the fix will target the wrong thing.

The through-line

Why it compounded

Nearly every bug in this batch was a case of something assumed where it could have been observed. A branch name printed instead of read. A path chosen instead of derived from the type that determines it. A page's identity taken from a variable instead of from the file. A budget cap applied without being announced.

The pattern is why they chained: each silent assumption produced output that looked correct, so the next step accepted it. Making them loud is most of the fix — three of these changes add nothing but an error where there used to be a shrug.

The practical difference: capturing a batch of sources in one sitting and reviewing the PRs later — wakil's own stated model, and the exact thing that didn't work — is now something the tool can actually do.

Ten pull requests, stacked in merge order from #193 to #202. Three ADR-worthy decisions recorded; four entries added to the development and troubleshooting logs.

1	# Resolve all open wakil issues — concurrent execution plan
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	`ebridges/wakil` has **36 open issues and zero open PRs**. Reading them end to end, they
6	are not 37 independent papercuts — they are roughly five failure clusters, and the
7	severe ones compound. The 2026-08-03/05 `kb-professional` engagement is the forcing
8	function: across ~8 transcript ingests the operator hand-repaired *every single one*,
9	and several issues are corroborated 4–6 times in their own comment threads.
10	
11	The compounding chain, as reported:
12	
13	> `ingest transcript` double-wraps the input (#172) → operator `git mv`s the file to fix it →
14	> `enrich` hard-fails because `sources.raw_text_path` still points at the old path (#178) →
15	> operator abandons `enrich` and hand-writes every downstream page.
16	
17	And separately:
18	
19	> `prepare_landing` switches onto the source's branch → minutes of model work → a concurrent
20	> `wakil mcp serve` process checks out `main` (#182) → `land_ingestion` commits to whatever
21	> HEAD *now* is, and prints the branch it *intended* (#181) → `gh pr create` with no `--head`
22	> opens the PR against yet another branch (#180).
23	
24	Root causes are confirmed at file:line (below), so this plan is about **sequencing and
25	parallelism**, not discovery. The intended outcome: the ingest→enrich→land pipeline becomes
26	trustworthy enough that a batch of sources can be captured in one sitting and reviewed later
27	as PRs — which is wakil's own stated model, and is exactly what currently breaks.
28	
29	### Decisions taken (confirmed with the user)
30	
31	| Decision | Choice |
32	|---|---|
33	| Scope | Fix all bugs + enhancements with clear user impact; **triage-comment** the speculative/blocked ones rather than build them |
34	| Execution | Parallel worktrees, with a serialized merge train for shared-file lanes |
35	| #174 timezone | `timezone:` key in `.wakil/config.yaml`, defaulting to the system local zone; DB timestamps stay UTC |
36	| #182 isolation | Advisory lock under `state_root` **plus** a HEAD assertion before commit (no auto-worktrees — those depend on #168 and carry their own documented hazard) |
37	
38	---
39	
40	## The hard constraint that shapes everything
41	
42	`src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py` is **3,424 lines** and is touched by five of the twelve
43	lanes. `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` already records the exact failure mode:
44	
45	> *"Stacked same-file refactor PRs from a shared base conflict on sequential merge even when
46	> the functions they touch don't overlap"* — PRs #109/#110/#111, all on `ingest_service.py`.
47	
48	So: **lanes that share a file form a serialized track; tracks run concurrently with each
49	other.** Five tracks, deepest is five lanes.
50	
51	Rejected: splitting `ingest_service.py` into modules first. It is a large, risky diff with no
52	user-visible value, and CLAUDE.md's prime directive says don't. The train costs one rebase per
53	lane; the split costs a full-file reconciliation against every lane at once.
54	
55	**Alembic revision numbers are reserved up front** so parallel lanes can't create competing
56	heads: `0008` → Lane W, `0009` → Lane S, `0010` → Lane M.
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Design-pass refinements (folded in after plan approval)
61	
62	A follow-up design pass verified two claims against live code and changed three decisions:
63	
64	- **#179 reproduced exactly.** `'**[00:36]** — Eddie: hi'` → `'**** — Eddie: hi'`. Bare `'**00:36**'`
65	  is untouched by both regexes. Confirms the correction already noted in Lane C.
66	- **#175's premise is wrong.** `_dialogue_from_segments:3082` *already* merges consecutive
67	  same-speaker segments and emits `**Speaker**: text` paragraphs, **not** bullets. The pasted
68	  evidence is consistent with MacWhisper's diarization flip-flopping mid-turn (contiguous runs of
69	  length 1, so merging is a no-op). **Blocked on getting a real `.whisper` fixture** into
70	  `tests/fixtures/` before any code is written — otherwise we'd fix the wrong thing.
71	- **Return-branch (#181b):** delete `LandingContext.original_branch` outright and always return to
72	  the repo's default branch, rather than returning to the just-committed branch.
73	  `ensure_clean_for_branch` already guarantees a clean tree, so the shell's incidental branch
74	  carries no information wakil needs; freezing it *is* the bug.
75	- **Commit timeout (#171):** `WAKIL_GIT_COMMIT_TIMEOUT` env var, default 600s — not a CLI flag,
76	  not a workspace-config key (signing setup is a *machine* property), and **not** TTY detection
77	  (`isatty()` is False under `wakil mcp serve` and `CliRunner`, so it would shorten the timeout
78	  exactly where a GUI signing prompt is still possible).
79	- **Lock (#182):** `fcntl.flock`, keyed on **`root_path`, not `state_root`** — two linked worktrees
80	  of one repo have independent indexes and must stay concurrent. `flock` over an `O_EXCL` PID file
81	  specifically because the kernel drops it when the holder dies: no TTL, no liveness probe, no
82	  reaper. **MCP must not hold the lock across `prepare`→`apply`** (cross-turn, 1-hour cache TTL,
83	  no guaranteed apply → every abandoned proposal would deadlock the workspace); instead
84	  `enrich_apply` re-acquires and re-runs the already-idempotent `prepare_landing`.
85	- **Cluster B adds no model call**, so no `FakeClient` construction site changes — the single
86	  biggest cost avoided. Keep it that way.
87	- **Second merge bottleneck:** `tests/unit/test_ingest_service.py` is 3,825 lines with the same
88	  conflict profile. Append each PR's tests at the **end of the file**, converting most conflicts
89	  into trivial append/append.
90	- **Likeliest red-suite surprise:** existing tests assert UTC-derived dates in filenames. Pin
91	  `TZ=UTC` + `time.tzset()` in `tests/conftest.py` as part of Lane C's date work.
92	
93	### Concrete merge order
94	
95	```
96	A4 → B1 → A1 → B2 → A2 → B3 → A3 → A5 → B4 → B5
97	```
98	
99	`A4` = commit timeout (#171, independent, merge first). `A1` = checked git reads. `A2` = HEAD
100	assertion + return-to-default (#181). `A3` = exact head/base PR (#180). `A5` = advisory lock (#182).
101	`B1` = frontmatter-aware capture + `clean_transcript` gating (#172+#179). `B2` = timezone (#174).
102	`B3` = collision policy (#173). `B4`/`B5` = whisper (#175, fixture-blocked).
103	
104	Interleaving keeps neither cluster stale against `main`. Order-sensitive edges only:
105	`A4` first, `A1→A2→A3→A5`, `B1→B5`.
106	
107	---
108	
109	## Tracks (run concurrently; sequential within a track)
110	
111	```
112	Track 1  ingest_service.py train   C ──► E ──► S ──► Q ──► N
113	Track 2  git landing               G
114	Track 3  workspace identity        W ──► I
115	Track 4  memory + dream            M ──► D
116	Track 5  repo hygiene + triage     H, T   (independent, any time)
117	```
118	
119	`W` must land before `C` rebases (both add a field to `WorkspaceConfig`).
120	`G` must land before `S`/`M` rebase (all touch `cli/main.py` + `mcp/tools.py`).
121	Both are cheap one-file rebases, not reconciliations.
122	
123	---
124	
125	# Fixes, ordered by impact
126	
127	## ▲ Tier 1 — Silent data corruption (nothing downstream is trustworthy until these land)
128	
129	### Lane G — git landing & session isolation · #181, #180, #171, #182
130	Branch `fix/git-landing-correctness`. Files: `app/git_service.py`, `integrations/git.py`,
131	`integrations/github.py`, new `app/session_lock.py`, `cli/main.py:333` (`_land_written_files`),
132	`mcp/tools.py:300` (`_land`).
133	
134	| # | Root cause (confirmed) | Fix |
135	|---|---|---|
136	| #181a | `land_ingestion` (`git_service.py:175`) calls `git.stage_and_commit` (`:207`) without ever checking HEAD. `context.branch` is only used for the *printed message* — "Committed X on Y" is a label, not an observation. | Assert `inspect_git().branch == context.branch` immediately before `stage_and_commit`; on mismatch, re-checkout the intended branch, and if that fails raise `GitServiceError` rather than committing. |

content.text:
Done for this run. Working tree clean, everything pushed.

## What I delivered

**1. The plan** — `~/.claude/plans/i-want-to-resolve-quizzical-shamir.md`. All 36 open issues (not 37) mapped to 12 lanes across 5 concurrent tracks, ordered by impact, root causes confirmed at file:line. The binding constraint was `ingest_service.py` (3,424 lines, touched by 5 lanes) — your own `DEVELOPMENT.md` records PRs #109/#110/#111 conflicting on that exact file, so those lanes form a serialized merge train while the rest run in parallel.

**2. Fourteen issues fixed, ten PRs** — two independent chains, merge each in order:

- **git**: [#193](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/193) → [#195](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/195) → [#196](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/196) — closes #171, #180, #181, #182
- **capture/enrich**: [#194](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/194) → [#197](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/197) → [#198](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/198) → [#199](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/199) → [#200](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/200) → [#201](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/201) → [#202](https://github.com/ebridges/wakil/pull/202) — closes #172, #173, #174, #176, #178, #179, #183, #186, #187, #188

675 tests passing, `ruff` and `ty` clean on every branch. All of Tier 1 done; nothing in the data-integrity tier remains.

**3. The article** — `~/wakil-repairs.html`, open it in a browser. Artifacts need a claude.ai login this session doesn't have (it's using `apiKeyHelper`), so it's a standalone styled page instead.

## Three things worth your attention

**#176 was wakil's bug, not the model's.** `prepare_enrichment` cut its input at 24,000 chars with a bare slice and told nobody. Your 28-minute transcript exceeded it, so the model made a true statement about the input it received — which you read as a false claim about your recording.

**#179 is partly misfiled.** A bare `**00:36**` never reproduced; only the bracketed form was destroyed. #175's premise is also wrong — `_dialogue_from_segments` already merges same-speaker segments. It needs a real `.whisper` fixture before anyone writes code, or the fix targets the wrong thing.

**#202 carries a measured regression.** One rubric item in a pre-existing eval, 3/3 fail on my branch vs. 1/1 pass on main. Adding skill guidance degraded an unrelated early step. Two rounds of tuning each traded one failure for the other, so I stopped — per your own recorded guidance about heuristics that swap failure modes — and documented all four measurements in the PR. That trade is your call.

## What's left

22 issues, all mapped to lanes and branch names in the plan, none in the data-integrity tier. The largest remaining items are #168 (workspace identity), #170/#190, and the enhancement lanes. Say the word and I'll continue down the plan.
